title: Ex 3.4 #7 · Odd digits first, then even digits
prompt: Use each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 exactly once to form a 9-digit number in which all the odd digits come first (on the left), followed by all the even digits, as in 975318642. How many such numbers are there?
answer_format: A whole number, or an expression for it like 26^4, 10!/7! or binom(10, 3). P(n, k) and C(n, k) work too.

mistakes.hint: The odd block and the even block are arranged independently: every order of the odd digits goes with every order of the even digits. Multiply rather than add.
That counts every arrangement of the nine digits, ignoring the odd-then-even rule.
You arranged the odd digits, but the even digits can also go in different orders.

hints: The first five positions hold the odd digits 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and the last four hold 2, 4, 6, 8.
Arrange each group within its own block, then combine the two counts.
solution: The five odd digits fill the first five positions in any order: $5! = 120$ ways. The four even digits fill the last four positions: $4! = 24$ ways.
By the multiplication principle there are $5! \cdot 4! = 120 \cdot 24 = 2880$ such numbers.

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses factorials and the multiplication principle (Section 3.4).
